extracted.intended_audience: scientists and science communicators who want to communicate science online / engage public audiences
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for scientists and science communicators on using websites, blogs, and social media to reach and engage public audiences; includes platform selection, identity/credibility, conversational norms, sharing dynamics, and network strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define your audience / use demographics to choose platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use audience-demographic information (for example, from the Pew Internet Project) to help define your audience for online communication and decide which platforms are best suited to your goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the audiences each platform affords you as a communicator; consult platform-specific demographic data and the provided weblinks when selecting where to communicate. Audience definition drives platform selection and message design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the goal–audience–message framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Explore ways to apply the goal-audience-message framework to social media and online platforms when planning communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with clear goals, identify target audiences, and craft messages appropriate to that audience and platform. This framework should guide platform choice, content style, and engagement tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website: credible, in-depth information hub
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a website as a credible source for public access to your research and expertise with opportunity to present in-depth information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Websites are most limited for active engagement as a standalone platform but can incorporate social media. Typical audience: individuals with more positive views about science and higher self-reported knowledge about science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blog: informal, conversational, topic-focused space
rubrics_metrics.description: Use blogs as a more informal, casual web-space dedicated to particular topics; they offer the opportunity to communicate and converse about a given topic rather than just disseminate information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blogs are among the most in-depth and informational platforms for communicating scientific topics conversationally. Typical audience: publics already interested in and knowledgeable about science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media: real-time interpersonal engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use social media for real-time, interpersonal communication and direct engagement with a wide range of audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social media offers maximum potential for public engagement through connected platforms. Typical audience: ubiquitous among younger adults and common among adults for science news consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple connected, complementary platforms strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ multiple connected, complementary platforms (e.g., Twitter, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, blogs) to build a social media presence while choosing platforms that best fit your goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain presence across platforms when useful, but make deliberate choices—e.g., Facebook can be useful for self-branding while Twitter may be better for conversational purposes. Consider workload and whether multiple platforms serve the same goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present a credible identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Present yourself as a credible source of information on social media; credibility is important for public engagement and science communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assert credibility by linking to affiliated institutions in social media profiles and making professional credentials and institutional associations visible (example: include institutional affiliation in Twitter profile).

rubrics_metrics.name: Match conversation dynamics and pace to platform and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the pace and dynamics of conversations differ across platforms (e.g., Twitter facilitates real-time discussion; slower-paced platforms demand less immediate attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for time constraints—platforms demanding immediate attention may limit what you can convey. Move discussions to other media for more extensive dialogue, and involve other experts/communicators to share the burden of engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design content for sharing (understand emotional drivers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharing (and potential virality) is influenced by emotions—particularly awe, anger, or anxiety—and by surprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting content, consider emotional resonance and elements of surprise that increase the likelihood content will be shared; note that 'virality' does not mean universal reach and is probabilistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider network structure and relationship flow
rubrics_metrics.description: When selecting and using platforms, consider goals for building relationships and the structure (how many connections and your position) and flow (strength of ties) of your networks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether you want smaller networks where you are central (useful for citizen science) or larger networks for broad layperson reach. Remember weak ties often provide greater reach across different networks than strong ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage endorsements and reputation signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that users rely on endorsements to gauge reputation; reputation can be a characteristic of content as well as users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use platform-specific endorsement metrics (likes, retweets, favorites, views) strategically to build and demonstrate reputation; monitor and cultivate endorsements as signals of credibility and reach.
